title: Biweekly Investment Insights: Earnings remain the clear driver for equity returns, yet risk underdelivering
author: Yanni Angelakos
description: Markets have largely traded sideways over the past two months as investors awaited a new catalyst. With Q2 earnings season underway, attention is shifting to whether strong corporate earnings can continue supporting equity markets. While earnings growth expectations remain robust, particularly for semiconductors, elevated valuations leave markets vulnerable if results disappoint. Investors are also closely watching whether significant AI-related investment will translate into meaningful returns. Recent market trends show a broadening of equity performance, with value stocks, small caps, and equal-weighted indexes outperforming. As earnings season progresses, inflation trends and macroeconomic developments will remain key factors shaping market direction.
content: AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Key Takeaways Epicenter of YTD equity story—semiconductors—2026 estimated EPS growth rate of 100%+ YoY. An increasingly high earnings bar with estimated AI capex of $5.5 trillion through 2030 Equal-weighted U.S. equity indexes, small caps, and the value factor have outperformed since the recent equity highs on June 2nd Softer June CPI and PPI readings help market’s near-term Fed rate hike angst As hypothesized in our May 21 st piece , equities have mostly traded sideways over the past two months as the markets awaited the next catalyst. From a fundamental perspective, that catalyst has likely arrived in the form of Q2 earnings which could set the tone for equities heading into the fall. Earnings growth is still expected to be very strong for broader U.S. equities and, even more so, for semiconductors, per our Biweekly Chart in Focus. While U.S. earnings and the AI theme have underpinned equities—keeping us constructive—the risk is that these lofty U.S. earnings expectations underdeliver. This could leave equities vulnerable in the near-term, amidst elevated valuations, though valuations are lower from the start of the year given the strong earnings story. Where is the AI theme susceptible? If estimated AI capex of $5.5 trillion (J.P. Morgan) through 2030 fails to result in a meaningful ROI for companies-namely, the hyperscalers. This would result in free cash flow and profitability headwinds, likely leading to a scaling back of capex intentions. This, in turn, could hurt the insatiable demand for chips from semiconductor companies. Biweekly Chart in Focus: PHLX Semiconductor Index (SOX) 2026 estimated EPS growth rates vs. average of 2023-2025 EPS growth rates (YoY%) in monthly intervals Since the recent U.S. equity highs on June 2 nd , U.S. semis are lower by 10%, and value and small caps have outperformed growth and large caps, respectively. Concurrently, a Morgan Stanley U.S. long/short momentum basket fell by 22% on a rolling 3-week basis—its largest decline since March 2021. Despite notable drawdowns in equity leadership recently—some profit taking was inevitable—headline U.S. indexes are still up solidly YTD. This illustrates a broadening in U.S. equity returns as respective equal-weighted indexes are in-line/outperforming their cap-weighted brethren. Looking further under the surface, while index level volatility is subdued, stock-specific volatility is extreme—speaking further to shifting undercurrents in the markets. With over 50% of broad U.S. equity market cap set to report Q2 earnings over the next two weeks, investors will be looking for another “show me” moment for equities. The bottom-up insights that investors will glean this earnings season will be balanced by the ongoing top-down dynamics such as inflation trends—June’s were softer—and the resurgence of military actions between the U.S. and Iran which factor into oil prices (+24% MTD), and play out in real-time via rates markets (Treasury 10-year yields at 2-month highs, over 4.6%) and Federal Reserve rate expectations. Details Strong earnings outlook coupled with the latest AI jitters The driver of U.S. equity returns has, of course, been the AI-fueled earnings story: as of July 10 th , Nasdaq-100® earnings growth was 48.5% over the prior 12 months, multiple expansion was -17.8%—resulting in a total return of 31.5% (factoring in residuals). With the strong earnings growth, Nasdaq-100 NTM P/E has gone from 25.6x on January 1 st to 24.7x as of July 10 th (per FactSet data). Per Figure 2, S&P 500 rolling next 12-month estimated EPS growth is 32% YoY—levels seen only following deep earnings recessions during 2008-2009 and briefly in early 2020; the prior, more mid-cycle high was around 22% in 2018. Figure 2: S&P 500 12-month forward estimated EPS growth rate (YoY%) The latest market paranoia around the AI capex trajectory came on July 17 th when Chinese AI startup, Moonshot, released Kimi K3. This model reportedly rivals OpenAI and Anthropic models (Figure 3) at a lesser cost, which reignited DeepSeek fears from January 2025. We suspect that the markets will likely have to endure waves of competitive rivals launching new, efficient models, and reportedly more inexpensive—this is simply an evolution of any new technology, product, or service. Yet it nevertheless brings into question just how much AI infrastructure spending is needed. However, it is not only the staggering estimates of AI capex to which investors pay attention—J.P. Morgan estimates $5.5 trillion in AI spend through 2030—but the funding sources as well (Figure 4). The mega cap tech space and hyperscalers are shifting from funding via cash flows to borrowing in the corporate debt market and through other financing channels. While the profit margins and balance sheets of Nasdaq-100 companies remain relatively strong per Nasdaq Index Insights , investors are likely to closely monitor company fundamentals should enterprise AI platforms fail to spur sufficient revenue. Figure 3: Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (higher is better) Figure 4: Anticipated AI capex funding sources through 2030 (in trillions) Broadening equity returns The recent sell-off in the AI ecosystem has been in flight since the June 2 nd U.S. equity highs as investors have looked elsewhere given lofty earnings and AI capex expectations and assumptions (Figure 5). This has pushed the market cap-weighted indexes to weaken on a YTD basis—though with still solid returns in 2026—and equal-weighted indexes to outperform (Figure 6). Figure 5: Equity themes YTD and since the recent June 2nd highs Figure 6: YTD % returns across market cap- and equal-weighted U.S. equity indexes Given the presence of AI-linked names in the long momentum baskets, Morgan Stanley’s U.S. momentum long/short index experienced its largest drawdown over a 3-week period since the March 2021 (Figure 7). Equity volatility at the index level remains subdued with the VIX under 18 and below its 5-year average of around 19. However, individual stock volatility, as measured by VIXEQ, hit its highest since March 2020 and its spread to VIX reached its highest on record going back to June 2014. So, while overall market volatility remains low, single-stock volatility is extremely elevated as investors digest more idiosyncratic risks. Is this a harbinger of weaker forward equity returns? Not according to history over the past 10 years: per Bloomberg, the S&P 500 has returned an average of 11.7% in the ensuing three months after VIXEQ eclipsed 50—it closed at 50.4 on July 21 st . Figure 7: Long/short U.S. momentum factor index on a rolling 15-day basis An inflation respite June CPI came in well below expectations, with headline CPI falling 0.4% MoM and +3.5% YoY (vs. +3.9% consensus). Core CPI was flat MoM and +2.6% YoY, driven primarily by a sharp drop in gasoline prices—the largest monthly decline since 2022—which more than offset still-elevated shelter and services costs. June PPI similarly surprised to the downside, with headline PPI falling  0.3% MoM and rising 5.5% YoY (vs. +6.2% consensus). Core PPI ex-food and energy rose just 0.2% MoM and 4.7% YoY (vs. +0.3% and +5.1% consensus, respectively), as a 6.4% MoM plunge in energy prices drove the broad deceleration. June’s PCE report, the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, will be released on July 30th—a day after the Fed’s next meeting—with consensus estimates also calling for a cooling in the headline and core readings. Despite CPI and PPI YoY indicators still hovering near multi-year highs (Figure 8), this was a needed reprieve for Fed fund futures pricing. Before the most recent inflation reads, markets were pricing in a 43% chance of a hike at the July 29th meeting vs. around 26% as of this writing. Headlines regarding a more concrete resolution or agreement between the U.S and Iran will likely remain volatile in the interim. However, if taking our cues from market-based inflation indicators (Figure 9), they continue to portend for an aversion of the left tail-risk scenarios of a more protracted and prolonged conflict which could retest the April highs in oil prices. title: Q&A: How Nasdaq Verafin and Q6 Cyber are Moving Fraud Prevention Upstream
author: Nasdaq Newsroom
description: The dark web is a hotbed of activity for fraudsters targeting banks and credit unions of all sizes. This activity often precedes actual fraud attempts by days, weeks and even months. Nasdaq Verafin and Q6 Cyber are collaborating to change the fraud-prevention timeline with this new partnership.
content: The dark web is a hotbed of activity for fraudsters targeting banks and credit unions of all sizes. This activity often precedes actual fraud attempts by days, weeks and even months. By the time a stolen or altered check is presented for fraudulent deposit at a bank or credit union, it's usually been on the dark web for over a week. Financial institutions and their customers have long been at a structural disadvantage, only able to see threats once they surface as fraudulent transactions. Liam Cooney, Head of Partnerships and Business Development at Nasdaq Verafin, and Eli Dominitz, Founder and CEO of Q6 Cyber, sat down with the Nasdaq Newsroom to explain more on how the two companies are collaborating to change the fraud-prevention timeline with this new partnership . Q: What does this collaboration between Nasdaq Verafin and Q6 do and what do you envision will be the impact on fraud prevention? Cooney (Verafin): Nasdaq Verafin's financial crime management technology platform serves more than 2,800 banks and credit unions. By working with Q6 Cyber, we can identify fraud and scams for our customers much earlier in the life cycle and disrupt financial crime with a higher degree of accuracy. This will help our customers and their end customers prevent potential losses. The signals that Eli and his team detect are extremely predictive of emerging fraud and scam attacks, and together with our platform, we can help our customers mitigate these threats earlier. Dominitz (Q6): What Liam said is by far the biggest impact. We have dark web data, which extends far beyond a bank and credit unions traditional defense perimeter, and Verafin has incredible transaction and counterparty data from their consortium network. Bringing those signals together will enable a new class of fraud prevention capabilities. Q: Eli, Q6 has spent a decade inside these dark web communities. What do they actually look like from the inside? Dominitz (Q6): It looks like an industry, because it is one. Dark web marketplaces have seller ratings, escrow, refund policies, and customer support. There are specialists at every step. For example, when it comes to check fraud, there are people who steal the checks, people who alter them, people who recruit the mules who deposit them — and they share techniques, even account balance information, with each other in real time. The dark web isn’t neat layers you can browse or crawl; it’s closer to a cave system — irregular passages and sealed entrances, where access is earned over years by people with reputations and histories inside those communities. Q: You've described Q6 Cyber's intelligence as predictive. What does that mean in practice? Dominitz (Q6): Take checks for example: our threat intelligence allows us to quickly identify that a check has been stolen, usually from the mail but it could be anywhere, and is being advertised for sale on the dark web. We also know that customers are likely to face subsequent types of fraud, such as social engineering, so the signal can be used to turn on other controls, too. Q: Given all of the things your team sees from the inside, what’s the most surprising thing your team has found for sale recently? Dominitz (Q6): Doing this for more than 10 years, it’s difficult for us to be surprised. But I’ll give you some interesting anecdotes. A few weeks ago, one of our analysts found a check advertised on a criminal marketplace with a face value just north of $1.6 million — a real check, drawn on a school board’s account, payable to a vendor. But nobody is walking into a branch to cash a $1.6 million check. The face value isn’t the prize — the account is. One check becomes a template, and one template can support dozens of fraud attempts: convincing counterfeits, altered payment instructions, or a phone call to someone in accounts payable that sounds legitimate because the caller knows things only an insider should. Meanwhile, the organization usually has no idea its details are circulating. When the institution holding that account receives our alert while the check is still just a listing, the story ends very differently. Cooney (Verafin): And that’s a good example of why we’re bringing this intelligence directly into our Nasdaq Verafin platform. A signal like that is never just one alert about one check — delivered inside the same workflow our customers already use to investigate cases, it tells the fraud team which account, which customer, and where to look next. Q: Walk us through what happens after a check like that gets listed. What do the next ten days look like? Dominitz (Q6): It moves quickly. The check is posted for sale today. A fraudster purchases it tomorrow, takes a couple of days to alter it, then deposits it. We know from years of experience that on average, seven to 10 days after we alert a client, they will see a fraudulent attempt with that check, usually after it’s been altered. That time window is everything. Because we are monitoring the dark web 24x7, 365 days a year, we collect the check and deliver an alert to our client the moment it surfaces. Banks and credit unions that receive our alerts have a critical time advantage to stop the check, close the account, alert the customer, and whatever else they feel is appropriate before there’s a deposit attempt. Q: Check fraud is just one part of the partnership, but what else does this cover? Dominitz (Q6): This partnership will start with check fraud detection, but we will expand to enable financial institutions to get ahead of most of the fraud attacks they are primarily concerned with. Every day we detect signals on the dark web suggesting that specific financial institutions are being targeted, and that specific accounts, whether a debit card, online banking credentials, or a check, have been compromised and are being targeted. These accurate and specific signals tell us exactly where the threats are highest and precede fraud attempts by days or weeks, allowing financial institutions to take action quickly to eliminate fraud. Q: Why is fraud growing so quickly? Dominitz (Q6): It's easy now to commit fraud remotely, with everything happening online. Technology is making things simpler and cheaper. Manufacturing documents or fake IDs, for example, is much easier with AI. Consumer and business data is widely available, and the technology to perpetrate attacks is also for sale. The economics are attractive to bad actors, and they can operate at a high degree of scale and complexity. Cooney (Verafin): That's why you need partnerships like this. If you wait until the point of payment, you're defending against more attacks than you ought to, and it ties up resources. Q: Most people assume protections like multi-factor authentication keep their accounts safe. What are you seeing that challenges that? Dominitz (Q6): The most sophisticated attacks we track are designed to be silent. We see malware that lets a fraudster log in from the customer’s own infected device — so the session comes from a trusted machine, with the expected device and browser fingerprints, and passes the authentication controls institutions rely on. We see tooling that pairs a victim’s phone to a computer the fraudster controls, so one-time codes sent by text are readable the moment they arrive, without the victim clicking a thing. And we see criminals sit quietly inside a compromised email inbox for weeks, reading and redirecting, before any money moves. None of that shows up in transaction data until the attempt is already underway. But the signals show up much earlier — in the communities where these tools are sold, tested, and bragged about. That’s where we sit. Cooney (Verafin): It’s worth being clear that the fraud stack at these institutions isn’t broken — a high-performance engine runs on whatever fuel it’s given. What this partnership does is feed that engine earlier, better fuel: signals from before the transaction ever happens. Q: What made this the right collaboration to pursue now? Cooney (Verafin): We are always looking for partnerships that help unlock core and new value propositions for our customers. In today’s landscape, fraud and scams are moving faster than ever before, whether that’s being driven by the use of AI by criminals or increasingly faster movement of money. Anything we can do to help our customers detect potential fraud before a transaction is even attempted moves us closer to cutting off fraud at the source. Q: What should customers expect from the integration itself? Cooney (Verafin): They'll be able to see Q6 alerts in the Nasdaq Verafin platform. We're doing the leg work for our customers, allowing them to have a more holistic picture of fraud threats all in one place. We’re starting with integrating Q6’s threat intelligence for stolen checks, payment cards, and account takeovers into our platform, and will be looking to leverage the power of our consortium network and data to generate additional opportunities to detect other fraud indicators. The combination of the external data from the dark web and the internal data from our consortium network will undoubtedly unlock tremendous value for our entire customer base, while also creating an opportunity to extend these capabilities across our network of more than 2,800 banks and credit unions. Q: Can you share a moment where this intelligence changed the outcome for an institution? Dominitz (Q6): At one regional financial institution, over six months we identified 202 stolen checks circulating on underground sites, tied to 150 customer accounts. The face value on those checks was about $1.2 million — but the accounts behind them held more than $66 million at the time of our alerts. Because the institution knew before the deposit attempts, it could stop the checks, protect the accounts, and warn its customers — including about the follow-on fraud that typically targets those same account holders next, like social engineering. That’s the difference between an alert that arrives before the attempt and one that arrives with the loss. Cooney (Verafin): If we can multiply that across more than 2,800 banks and credit unions, you see why we’re excited. Offering these signals to every fraud team on our platform, in the workflow they already use, is how prevention has the potential to move upstream at scale while carrying significant opportunity to extend these capabilities across our existing customer base. Read more about the partnership between Nasdaq Verafin and Q6 .

title: Entity Management Software: Definition, Use Cases, Benefits, and Key Considerations
author: Nasdaq Capital Access Platforms
description: What is entity management software — and who is it for? Learn how organizations manage entity data, documentation, and governance‑related workflows.
content: Key Takeaways Entity management software is commonly used to centralize and organize legal entity information, including data spanning multiple jurisdictions. Many organizations use these platforms to support governance visibility, documentation management, and internal coordination across teams. Capabilities, features, and use cases vary widely depending on an organization’s size, structure, industry, and regulatory environment. Entity management software is not a substitute for legal or compliance advice, but may help support more consistent internal processes and recordkeeping. As governance and organizational complexity increases, some organizations evaluate purpose‑built entity management tools alongside existing legal, finance, and governance workflows.
